analyst:
Michigan enters the 2026 NCAA Tournament with a 29-2 overall record and a 19-1 Big Ten record after closing the regular season with a 90-80 Senior Day win over Michigan State on March 8, 2026. Michigan had already clinched the outright Big Ten title on February 27 with an 84-70 road win at No. 10 Illinois, and that win gave Dusty May’s team its 17th league victory at the time, a program record that it later extended to 19. The Wolverines also finished 10-0 in Big Ten road games, and their March 5 win at Iowa made them the first team in conference history to go 10-0 on the road in league play. Offensively, through mid-February Michigan was averaging 87.1 points per game, shooting .500 from the field, .349 from three, and posting 261 assists against 162 turnovers; by late January the staff notes described the attack as a “fast-paced, transition-driven, read-and-react system built around spacing, long-range shooting, and multiple ball-screen actions.”

The offensive identity is very specific. Dusty May’s own game notes label the scheme as spacing-heavy and ball-screen-based, and the roster construction matches it: point guard Elliot Cadeau organizes actions, while Yaxel Lendeborg and Aday Mara both function as frontcourt passers, not just finishers. By January 27, Michigan had already produced seven 20-assist games, including 31 assists in the season opener against Oakland, the program’s first 30-assist game in 33 years. Cadeau had 98 assists by that point and was the lead decision-maker, while Lendeborg had 61 assists and Mara 44, evidence that Michigan runs offense through dribble handoffs, short-roll reads, and interior facilitation instead of simple one-guard creation. Specific examples show the structure: in the January 23 win over Ohio State, Michigan generated a tip-jam sequence assisted by Lendeborg to Morez Johnson Jr.; in the February 27 win at Illinois, after Illinois cut the lead to 53-48, Michigan came out of a timeout and answered with a Lendeborg score through contact, then a 7-0 personal burst from Mara, showing how May uses timeout possessions to re-establish paint touches and interior passing. Against Michigan State on March 8, Michigan used an 11-0 second-half run highlighted by Trey McKenney scoring eight straight points, then out of a timeout with 2:39 left Lendeborg found Johnson on an alley-oop dunk, a clear example of set-play execution late.

Defensively, Michigan is not a soft drop team. The official scouting notes state that the Wolverines play an “active man-to-man scheme, switching both on- and off-ball screens,” generally exchanging across positions one through four while keeping more traditional coverages with the five. That fits the personnel: Mara had 51 blocks and was averaging 2.68 blocks per game by January 27, Lendeborg had 26 blocks, and Johnson had 24; together those three accounted for 101 of Michigan’s 117 blocks at that point. The numbers reflect the philosophy. Michigan led the Big Ten and ranked fourth nationally in blocks per game at 6.2, while holding opponents to 36.5 percent shooting, the second-lowest mark in the nation as of late January. The switchability plus rim protection showed up in results: Michigan beat No. 21 Auburn 102-72, No. 12 Gonzaga 101-61, and No. 24 USC 96-66, becoming the first team in AP poll history to win three straight games by 30-plus against ranked opponents. In the Illinois win, Mara’s block directly triggered a Roddy Gayle Jr. transition dunk. In the March 8 win over Michigan State, Michigan State failed to score on three straight possessions after the late alley-oop, and Michigan closed the game at the foul line.

May’s coaching philosophy is documented as collective and adjustment-driven. Michigan’s December notes say he emphasizes “collective excellence over individual heroics,” and his November notes quote his roster-building ideal as wanting “stars, not a star.” That shows up in the distribution of production: by mid-February, six different Wolverines had led the team in scoring in at least one game listed on the schedule, and nine players had already scored in the February 17 road win at No. 7 Purdue by the 4:17 mark of the first half. His in-game adjustment history is also concrete. Against Illinois on February 27, he used a timeout after the Illini’s second-chance surge cut the margin to five, and Michigan immediately stabilized with a Lendeborg three-point play and Mara’s 7-0 run. Against Michigan State on January 30, May challenged a foul on Lendeborg with 2:30 left; the call was overturned into a flagrant on the Spartans, Lendeborg hit two free throws, then added an and-one on the next sequence as Michigan re-extended control in an 83-71 road win. Against Michigan State again on March 8, the staff clearly found the right counter after a 61-61 tie with 11:51 left: McKenney became the focal scorer during the 11-0 run, and Michigan then executed through Lendeborg-Johnson action late.

Clutch and late-game execution is one of Michigan’s strongest tournament indicators. They beat Wake Forest 85-84 in overtime on November 11, with Cadeau assisting on the basket that tied the game late in regulation. They survived Penn State 74-72 on January 6, a game the program later described as one in which the Wolverines “narrowly remained unbeaten.” They beat No. 5 Nebraska 75-72 on January 27, and official notes called it a rally in the final three minutes. They won at No. 7 Michigan State 83-71 on January 30 after weathering the Spartans’ second-half push. They won at Iowa 71-68 on March 5 in a game with 14 lead changes and eight ties, then closed it in the final seconds. The only real late-game offensive failure against elite competition came in the 68-63 loss to No. 3 Duke on February 21: Michigan cut the lead to one with under four minutes left, but Duke led the entire second half and held on. That game revealed that when possessions bog down into half-court shotmaking without transition flow, Michigan can become more dependent on its frontcourt trio than on perimeter creation.

The key players are easy to identify. Lendeborg is the matchup problem and all-around fulcrum. By January 27 he was averaging 14.4 points, 7.2 rebounds, 3.2 assists, 1.4 blocks, and 1.5 steals while shooting 51.4 percent from the floor and 83.8 percent from the line. He scored 26 points and grabbed 12 rebounds at Michigan State on January 30, scored 21 in the Duke loss on February 21, and was the MVP of the Players Era Festival after averaging 17.3 points, 7.3 rebounds, 3.7 assists, 2.0 steals, and 1.3 blocks across wins over San Diego State, Auburn, and Gonzaga. Johnson is the force finisher. By January 27 he was averaging 13.7 points and 6.9 rebounds while shooting 68.7 percent from the field, which led the Big Ten and ranked third nationally. He scored 24-plus in back-to-back holiday games, including 26.5 points per game over that stretch, and had 19 points and 11 rebounds at Illinois on February 27. Mara is the interior anchor and passing center; by January 27 he was averaging 10.9 points, 7.1 rebounds, and 2.7 blocks, and by mid-February he had 66 total blocks at 2.8 per game. His standout games include 18 points, 13 rebounds, six assists, and five blocks vs. Wake Forest on November 11, plus a self-created 7-0 run at Illinois. Cadeau is the floor general, averaging 5.2 assists by late January and 5.5 by mid-February; he had 17 points at Purdue on February 17 and repeatedly appears as Michigan’s assist leader in big wins. McKenney is the bench scorer and late-clock shotmaker: he averaged 9.9 points by January 27, had 30 made threes by then, and his eight straight points fueled the decisive second-half run against Michigan State on March 8. Burnett remains the spacing guard, with 29 made threes by January 27 and a 31-point outburst against Penn State on February 5.

The notable wins show both ceiling and style. Auburn lost by 30 on November 25, Gonzaga by 40 on November 26, USC by 30 on January 2, Nebraska by three on January 27, Michigan State by 12 on January 30 and by 10 on March 8, Purdue by 11 on February 17, Illinois by 14 on February 27, and Iowa by three on March 5. The blowouts revealed the defensive ceiling and ball movement; the Nebraska, Penn State, and Iowa escapes revealed poise in ugly games; the Purdue and Illinois road wins showed they can beat top-10 caliber teams in hostile environments. The losses also matter. Duke beat Michigan 68-63 on February 21 in Washington, D.C., exposing that Michigan can be pulled into a slower half-court game where it struggles to regain the lead once trailing. TCU also pushed Michigan in a 67-63 game on November 14, another sign that lower-possession games can compress Michigan’s margin.

As for the head coach, Dusty May’s NCAA tournament history is now substantial. Michigan’s own game notes list his recent NCAA results as Final Four in 2023, First Round in 2024, and Sweet 16 in 2025 before this current 2026 Michigan run began. At Michigan specifically, he took the Wolverines to the Sweet 16 in 2025 after a 27-10 first season. Entering the 2026 tournament, that gives him a documented history of building teams that can win multiple games when their defensive versatility and ball-screen offense are functioning. The scouting bottom line is straightforward: Michigan is not just talented; it is structurally difficult to prepare for because Cadeau initiates, Lendeborg and Mara pass, Johnson finishes, and the defense can switch one through four while still erasing mistakes at the rim. Against tournament teams with limited size, Michigan can bury opponents with pace, passing, and paint pressure. Against elite shotmakers who can force static half-court possessions, as Duke did on February 21, the Wolverines look more vulnerable.

Michigan enters the 2026 NCAA Tournament with a profile that is unmistakably elite and unusually balanced. Through games of March 15, 2026, the Wolverines were 31-3 and ranked No. 2 in the NCAA NET, with an 17-3 record in Quad 1 games, 5-0 in Quad 2, 6-0 in Quad 3, and 3-0 in Quad 4. That résumé is not just strong; it is structurally dominant. Michigan has accumulated high-end wins at a rate typical of a No. 1 seed while avoiding the bad losses that usually drag otherwise strong predictive profiles back toward the pack. ([ncaa.com](https://www.ncaa.com/rankings/basketball-men/d1/ncaa-mens-basketball-net-rankings))

On the predictive side, Michigan also grades as a national title-level team. ESPN’s BPI page for the 2025-26 season listed Michigan No. 2 nationally with a BPI of 24.9 as of the March 7, 2026 update. ESPN also showed Michigan at 28-2 at that snapshot, with offensive and defensive BPI components of 12.2 and 12.7 respectively, which is notable because it implies near-equal strength on both sides rather than a lopsided offense-first or defense-first construction. In other words, Michigan is not surviving on shot-making variance or on a single overwhelming unit; the team projects as complete. ([espn.com](https://www.espn.com/mens-college-basketball/bpi/_/season/2026?utm_source=openai))

KenPom’s exact subscription values were not fully accessible in search results, but multiple contemporaneous sources place Michigan in the very top tier nationally. NCAA.com’s March 1 feature explicitly said Michigan sat “ahead of the field by several car lengths on KenPom,” a remarkable description for a season this deep into conference play. Purdue’s January 2026 game notes, citing Bart Torvik, described Michigan as No. 1 nationally in overall efficiency at that point, with the nation’s No. 2 adjusted offense and No. 13 adjusted defense. Even allowing for some movement between January and Selection Sunday, the stable takeaway is that Michigan has spent essentially the entire second half of the season in the top handful nationally, with an offense safely in the top two or three and a defense in roughly the top 10-15 range. ([ncaa.com](https://www.ncaa.com/news/basketball-men/article/2026-03-01/what-make-questions-only-march-can-answer-mens-college-basketball?utm_source=openai))

Michigan’s raw team-stat efficiency supports that interpretation. On the official Michigan cumulative stats page through 34 games, the Wolverines had made 766 field goals on 1,547 attempts, including 227 made threes on 645 attempts. That translates to a 49.5% field-goal rate, 35.2% from three, and an estimated effective field-goal percentage of 56.9%. Their 3-point attempt rate was about 41.7%, indicating a modern, spacing-heavy shot mix rather than a purely interior attack. They had also attempted 265 free throws against 1,547 field-goal attempts, for an estimated free-throw rate of 17.1%. ([mgoblue.com](https://mgoblue.com/sports/mens-basketball/stats/2025-26))

That combination is analytically interesting. A 56.9% eFG% is strong enough for a top-tier offense, but the free-throw rate is modest for a team with this caliber of efficiency. Michigan is not bludgeoning opponents through foul pressure in the way some conventional “physical Big Ten contender” stereotypes would suggest. Instead, the Wolverines appear to be generating elite offense more through shot quality, conversion efficiency, and lineup balance than through overwhelming rim pressure or whistle-dependent scoring. The roster totals reinforce that. Michigan has multiple high-efficiency frontcourt scorers: Morez Johnson Jr. shot 62.8% from the field, Aday Mara 67.4%, and Yaxel Lendeborg 50.9% while also taking 150 threes and converting 35.3%. That is a highly unusual combination of size and spacing. ([mgoblue.com](https://mgoblue.com/sports/mens-basketball/stats/2025-26))

The offensive shape of the team diverges from simplistic eye-test assumptions. At first glance, Michigan’s size suggests an old-school interior offense, yet the statistical evidence points to a flexible attack: bigs who score efficiently, a meaningful perimeter volume rate, and enough shooting from multiple lineup spots to keep the floor open. Elliot Cadeau’s 189 assists against 82 turnovers gives the offense an organizer with a strong creation-to-mistake ratio, while Trey McKenney, L.J. Cason, and Nimari Burnett all add perimeter volume. This is not just a “throw it inside and crash” team. It is a multi-layered offense that can score with post efficiency, pick-and-roll orchestration, and secondary shooting. ([mgoblue.com](https://mgoblue.com/sports/mens-basketball/stats/2025-26))

On the glass, Michigan looks solid but not cartoonishly dominant. Using the available team rebounding totals, the Wolverines posted 388 offensive rebounds. Combining Michigan offensive boards with opponents’ defensive boards yields an estimated offensive rebounding rate of about 29.5%, which is good but not overwhelming. That matters because it suggests Michigan’s offense is less dependent on second chances than people may assume from the roster’s size. Again, the theme is efficiency through quality rather than brute force. ([mgoblue.com](https://mgoblue.com/sports/mens-basketball/stats/2025-26))

Strength of schedule also adds credibility. ESPN’s BPI page showed Michigan with a remaining SOS rank of 25th at the March 7 snapshot, while another ESPN sort page placed Michigan’s schedule strength around the low-20s nationally. Independent commentary cited Michigan’s schedule as seventh nationally in one advanced-metrics roundup. Even if those exact schedule measures are not identical, they point in the same direction: this profile was built against a clearly high-major, tournament-grade slate. The 17-3 Quad 1 record in the official NET sheet is the strongest confirmation of that underlying reality. ([espn.com](https://www.espn.com/mens-college-basketball/bpi/_/season/2026?utm_source=openai))

For recent form, the available evidence is also favorable. Michigan’s official notes entering mid-February said the Wolverines had won eight of their last 10. By March 15 they were 31-3 and still No. 2 in NET, indicating that any late-season turbulence was modest rather than structural. The broader reporting around Michigan emphasized not fragility but dominance: six wins over ranked opponents by double digits, plus a résumé strong enough that NCAA.com bracket projections elevated the Wolverines onto the No. 1 seed line in early February. The best synthesis is that Michigan did not merely peak early; it sustained elite two-way performance across the season’s middle and closing phases. ([mgoblue.com](https://mgoblue.com/documents/download/2026/2/9/20260209-bkm-notes-northwestern.pdf?utm_source=openai))

Where do the numbers most clearly diverge from conventional wisdom? First, Michigan’s offense seems more perimeter-structured and skill-based than its frontcourt-heavy optics imply, given the 41.7% three-point attempt rate. Second, the Wolverines’ efficiency does not appear to be driven by free throws, which runs against the default assumption that big, powerful teams must live at the line. Third, the defense may be slightly less suffocating than the résumé and win-loss record suggest; the accessible predictive references consistently portray the offense as the truly elite unit, with the defense very good rather than historically dominant. That distinction matters in March. Michigan’s statistical case is that of a top-two or top-three national team because the offense is devastating and the defense is comfortably good enough to support it, not because opponents are being erased every night. ([storage.googleapis.com](https://storage.googleapis.com/purduesports-com-prod/2026/01/09/YReQpcKA1tCB8x3QGyevpjQLFq2zqGF5XuF8jAnX.pdf?utm_source=openai))

Bottom line: Michigan’s 2026 tournament profile is that of a genuine championship favorite. The Wolverines pair a No. 2 NET résumé with a No. 2 BPI ranking, top-of-the-sport KenPom/Torvik standing, excellent shooting efficiency, a high-volume three-point diet, strong but not overreliant offensive rebounding, and a schedule résumé validated by both Quad 1 volume and predictive metrics. The most important forecast signal is not just that Michigan is great; it is that the Wolverines are great in a way that tends to travel in March: efficient offense, structural balance, lineup versatility, and enough defensive backbone to survive games in which the jumpers cool off. ([ncaa.com](https://www.ncaa.com/rankings/basketball-men/d1/ncaa-mens-basketball-net-rankings))
matchup-analyst:
Michigan is built to overwhelm teams with pace, size and continuous advantage creation, but the clearest way to attack them is to break the game into a half-court, shot-clock-heavy possession battle and make their big front line defend repeated perimeter actions. Through Feb. 12, Michigan was 23-1 while averaging 90.8 points per game on 51.0% shooting, assisting on 466 made baskets, and playing at one of the fastest tempos in the country. UM Hoops reported that Michigan’s average offensive possession lasted only 14.4 seconds, that the Wolverines ranked fourth nationally in tempo at 75.3 possessions per game, and that they scored 25.7 transition points per game, 7.8 more than No. 2 Michigan State. UM Hoops also noted that six of nine rotation players had an assist rate above 10%, which fits the tape: this is not a static isolation team, it is a read-and-react team that tries to turn rebounds, outlet passes, early seals and drag screens into fast paint touches and kickout threes. ([mgoblue.com](https://mgoblue.com/documents/download/2026/2/14/bkm-stats-2025-26.pdf))

The specific tactics that disrupt Michigan’s style are: 1) elite transition defense, 2) tempo suppression, 3) forcing long defensive possessions against spread shooting, and 4) making their guards finish under pressure instead of letting the frontcourt play off early advantages. UM Hoops identified Minnesota as the national leader in transition defense at just 6.3 transition points allowed per game and highlighted that Minnesota was also 358th in adjusted tempo, with Michigan having not played a game slower than 62 possessions in the Dusty May era. That matters because when Minnesota visited on Feb. 24, Michigan led only 32-28 at halftime, and that 32-point half was its lowest-scoring half of the season. That is the template: shrink the game, get back, and force Michigan to execute later in the clock. ([umhoops.com](https://umhoops.com/2026/02/24/game-28-minnesota-at-michigan-preview/?utm_source=openai))

Michigan’s press vulnerability is real enough to probe, even if it has usually survived it. The clearest evidence is ball security at the point of attack. Through Feb. 12, Michigan averaged 12.3 turnovers per game, and opponents forced games into turnover-heavy environments when they sped up Cadeau and the secondary ballhandlers. In the Nov. 14 win at TCU, Cadeau had 6 turnovers by himself; in the Feb. 11 comeback at Northwestern, Michigan still committed 12 turnovers despite winning; and against Wisconsin on Jan. 10, Michigan lost 91-88 while getting only 11 assists, with Cadeau committing 7 turnovers and the team producing 12 points off Wisconsin turnovers compared with allowing Wisconsin to score 15 second-chance points and 15 made threes. Those are not generic red flags: they show that if you heat the handlers and then finish possessions with rebounds, Michigan’s offense becomes less connected. ([mgoblue.com](https://mgoblue.com/documents/download/2026/2/14/bkm-stats-2025-26.pdf))

Zone vulnerability is harder to prove as a season-long weakness from public data, but the practical pressure point is visible: make Michigan settle for volume threes from the wrong shooters and eliminate paint-to-paint flow. Michigan as a team was excellent overall from three through Feb. 12 at 35.4%, but the shot distribution matters. Nimari Burnett was at 40-for-99 from three (40.4%) and Elliot Cadeau at 41-for-102 (40.2%), while Roddy Gayle Jr. was at 11-for-42 (26.2%) and Yaxel Lendeborg at 29-for-101 (28.7%). Wisconsin’s Jan. 10 upset is a good example of the kind of game a zone-oriented opponent would want: Michigan shot just 8-for-25 from three (32.0%) while Wisconsin bombed 15-for-33. If you zone selectively, tag the rollers, and close hard to Burnett/Cadeau while living with Gayle/Lendeborg above-the-break attempts, you can redirect the offense away from its best actions. ([mgoblue.com](https://mgoblue.com/documents/download/2026/2/14/bkm-stats-2025-26.pdf))

Preferred pace is obvious: Michigan wants an open-floor game. UM Hoops’ data that the Wolverines score 25.7 transition points per game is the single most important tactical stat in this profile. To force the opposite, the opponent must send two guards back on the shot, avoid live-ball turnovers, and use offense as defense by running long possessions. Minnesota’s 32-28 halftime game and TCU’s 67-63 final are named examples that Michigan can be dragged into a lower-possession contest. At TCU, Michigan won with frontcourt rebounding and defense rather than flow offense, which is not their preferred operating mode. ([umhoops.com](https://umhoops.com/2026/01/05/inside-michigans-13-0-start-the-blueprint-behind-the-dominance/))

The size and athleticism mismatches are unusual at every spot. At point guard, Elliot Cadeau is only 6-1, 180, so a bigger on-ball defender can body him; the counter is his 5.5 assists per game and 40.2% three-point shooting. At the 2/3, Burnett is 6-5 and Trey McKenney is a strong 6-4 scoring guard, while Roddy Gayle Jr. adds another physical wing. The frontcourt is the real problem: Yaxel Lendeborg led Michigan with 7.7 rebounds per game, Morez Johnson Jr. had 7.3, and Aday Mara had 6.9 while anchoring a team that averaged 42.0 rebounds and led the nation in defensive rebounds in January notes. Against smaller teams, that size produces paint points and second shots; against equally big or more mobile teams, the mismatch can flip because you can pull those bigs into space. Wisconsin exposed some of that by spacing the floor and hitting 15 threes, while Auburn in the 2025 NCAA Sweet 16 showed the longer-term blueprint: Auburn erased a 49-38 deficit, outscored Michigan 39-17 over the final 12:30, won the glass 48-33 with 19 offensive rebounds, and held Michigan to 21-of-59 shooting with only 6 assists. That game is from March 28, 2025, not this season, but it is still relevant as a tactical analogue for attacking big Michigan front lines with speed-plus-strength. ([espn.com](https://www.espn.com/mens-college-basketball/team/roster/_/id/130/sort/height/michigan-wolverines))

Isolation versus team offense: the public 2026 data available here strongly indicates Michigan leans team offense, not isolation. Through Jan. 8, Michigan had assisted on 63% of made field goals, and through Feb. 12 Cadeau averaged 5.5 assists while Lendeborg added 3.2 and Gayle 1.6. That is the most reliable percentage available from current team materials. I could not verify a current public Synergy isolation-usage percentage for the full 2025-26 team from an accessible primary source, so I will not invent one. The evidence we do have says Michigan prefers connected offense created by early push, paint touch, kickout, and big-to-big or guard-to-big passing rather than clearing a side repeatedly. ([mgoblue.com](https://mgoblue.com/documents/download/2026/1/8/20260108-bkm-notes-wisconsin.pdf))

Transition offense and defense frequency: current public team materials clearly support the offense side. UM Hoops reported 25.7 transition points per game and a 14.4-second average offensive possession. I could not verify a team transition-defense frequency percentage from an accessible 2026 primary source, but the best tactical evidence is indirect: Michigan’s defensive size and block rate are elite, yet teams that space and shoot can still stress them. Michigan was fourth nationally in blocks per game in the Jan. 8 notes, but Wisconsin scored 91 with 15 threes, and Northwestern reached 75 while building a 16-point lead before Michigan’s comeback. ([umhoops.com](https://umhoops.com/2026/01/05/inside-michigans-13-0-start-the-blueprint-behind-the-dominance/))

Coaching adaptability is a strength. Dusty May’s staff has repeatedly changed game texture midgame. Michigan’s notes document halftime-deficit wins at TCU (down 35-33, won 67-63), at Maryland (down 50-45, won 101-83), at Oregon (down 41-40, won 81-71), against No. 5 Nebraska (down 50-48, won 75-72), and later at Northwestern, where Michigan trailed by 16 in the second half before a 26-9 run and ultimately a 45-17 closing stretch over the final 14 minutes. That is not “mid-series” in the NBA sense, but in college terms it is strong evidence of in-game adjustment capacity. ([mgoblue.com](https://mgoblue.com/documents/download/2026/2/7/20260206-bkm-notes-ohio-state.pdf))

Concrete gameplan: To beat Michigan, you must make the game ugly and slow. First, send two defenders back on every shot and concede some offensive-rebound opportunities if needed; the priority is eliminating the 25.7 transition points per game that fuel their identity. Second, pick up Cadeau early and physically, because his playmaking organizes everything, but he has had high-turnover games like the 6-turnover night at TCU and 7-turnover game against Wisconsin. Third, shrink the floor versus Lendeborg/Mara/Johnson by zoning selectively or stunting hard from Gayle and Lendeborg, the weaker volume shooters. Fourth, offensively, run pick-and-pop and flare-heavy spacing actions to pull Michigan’s bigs away from the rim; Wisconsin’s 15-for-33 three-point game is the model. Fifth, finish possessions with rebounds, because when Michigan gets extra paint touches and quick outlets, the avalanche starts. Sixth, expect May to adjust, so your counter must be to stay committed to tempo control for 40 minutes, not 20. If you let Michigan turn the game into a running contest, their size-plus-skill profile usually snowballs. If you turn it into a 62-possession rock fight, make their guards score over set help, and win the three-point math, you give yourself a real path. ([umhoops.com](https://umhoops.com/2026/02/24/game-28-minnesota-at-michigan-preview/?utm_source=openai))
